conventional_description:
Traction alopecia is a form of hair loss caused by prolonged or repetitive tension on the hair follicles. It is most commonly seen along the hairline, temples, or where hair is pulled tightly in styles like braids, ponytails, weaves, or buns. The condition can be temporary if the tension is relieved early, but persistent pulling can damage follicles permanently, leading to scarring and irreversible hair loss.
Diagnosis is usually made by examining the pattern of hair loss and taking a history of hairstyling habits. A dermatologist may use a dermatoscope to assess follicle health. Standard advice is to avoid tight hairstyles, but once scarring has set in, regrowth is limited and treatments like minoxidil or hair transplant may be considered.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management focuses on removing the source of tension - loosening or changing hairstyles - and supporting regrowth with topical minoxidil. Anti-inflammatory medications or corticosteroid injections may be used if there is significant inflammation or scarring. In advanced cases where follicles have been destroyed, hair transplant surgery remains the only option for restoring hair in the affected areas.
tcm_understanding: In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the hair is considered the surplus of Blood, and its health reflects the state of the Kidney, Liver, and Spleen. When tight hairstyles pull on the hair, they create a local blockage of Qi and Blood, much like a tourniquet. Over time, this mechanical stagnation can combine with internal imbalances - such as Blood Stasis, Damp-Heat, or deficiencies of Kidney Essence and Blood - to weaken the hair roots and cause hair loss. TCM therefore treats traction alopecia not just by advising to loosen the hairstyle, but by identifying and correcting the underlying pattern that made the scalp vulnerable, using herbs, acupuncture, and dietary adjustments to restore free flow and nourishment to the follicles.
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by understanding your hairstyle habits, the tightness, and the duration of traction. They ask about the exact location of hair loss, any scalp pain or tenderness, and the feel of the hair-is it dry, brittle, oily, or itchy? They also explore your emotional state, energy levels, and digestion. The tongue’s color and coating, along with the pulse’s quality, provide the final clues that pinpoint the underlying pattern.
If the main complaint is a fixed, stabbing scalp tenderness where the hair was pulled, Blood Stagnation is likely. The hair may appear dull and dry. The tongue often shows a dark red or purplish body with possible stasis spots, and the pulse feels choppy or wiry. This pattern is very common because tight hairstyles directly block local blood circulation, starving the follicles.
When the scalp is oily, itchy, and flaky with heavy shedding, Damp-Heat is the prime suspect. You may also notice a bitter taste in the mouth, abdominal bloating, or sticky bowel movements. The tongue is typically red with a thick, greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is slippery and rapid. This pattern often flares up with rich, greasy, or spicy foods.
If emotional stress or frustration seems to trigger or worsen your hair loss, and you experience chest or rib-side distension, the pattern may be Liver Qi Stagnation turning into Blood Stasis. Hair loss can be patchy. The tongue may be dark or have a purplish hue, and the pulse is wiry and choppy. The practitioner will ask about your mood and any feeling of a lump in the throat.
Long-term traction can gradually exhaust Kidney Essence, leading to sparse, brittle hair and premature graying. Systemic signs like a sore lower back, weak knees, dizziness, or tinnitus often accompany the hair loss. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is deep and thin. This pattern is more common in chronic cases or with aging.
When the body’s overall Qi and Blood are insufficient, hair becomes fragile and sheds easily, often without much scalp pain. You may feel constantly tired, look pale, and have brittle nails. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is weak and thin. This pattern reflects a deeper constitutional weakness that fails to nourish the hair roots.
If your hair is dry, brittle, and prone to breaking, and your scalp feels slightly itchy, you may have Blood Deficiency generating Dry-Wind. Other signs include dizziness, dry skin, or a pale complexion. The tongue is pale, and the pulse is thin and choppy. This pattern often overlaps with Qi and Blood Deficiency but emphasizes a lack of moisture and blood to anchor the hair.

patterns.symptoms: ["Hair loss in a band or patch matching the traction line", "Fixed, stabbing pain in the scalp or ribcage", "Pain that is worse with pressure or at night", "Dark or purplish tongue with possible stasis spots", "Tenderness when touching the affected area"]
patterns.worse_with: Tight hairstyles (braids, ponytails, weaves), Emotional stress or frustration, Cold or wind exposure on the head, Prolonged sitting or inactivity
patterns.better_with: Loosening tight hairstyles, Gentle scalp massage, Warmth on the scalp, Light exercise that moves the neck and shoulders
patterns.why_this_happens: Tight hairstyles and persistent pulling create a physical blockage in the tiny vessels that feed the hair roots. This trapped blood fails to nourish the follicles, so the strands weaken, thin, and eventually fall out in the exact lines where the tension is greatest. The scalp often feels tender or stabbing because stagnant blood presses on the nerves.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple or dusky body, stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩, Sè) like a knife scraping bamboo, often with a wiry (弦, Xián) quality.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stagnation means the flow is physically stuck. Anything that increases pressure or constriction-like tight hairstyles, cold, or stress (which tightens the Liver Qi)-deepens the stasis and worsens pain and shedding. Gentle movement, warmth, and massage literally push the blood along, while loosening the hair removes the original cause. This is why simple daily habits can make a big difference.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Switch to loose, low-tension hairstyles immediately and avoid rubber bands, tight braids, or extensions. Gently massage the scalp with your fingertips for a few minutes daily to encourage blood flow. Add a little black vinegar to your diet-it helps move blood. Saffron (a pinch in warm water) and dark leafy greens also support healthy circulation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Scalp oily, sticky, and inflamed", "Itching and greasy dandruff that clings to the scalp", "Bitter taste and sticky sensation in the mouth", "Heavy, sluggish body, as if weighted down", "Loose, sticky stools that feel incomplete"]

patterns.better_with: Cool, dry weather, Frequent gentle hair washing, Light, non-greasy meals, Loosening tight hairstyles
patterns.why_this_happens: Tight hairstyles trap sweat and oil against the scalp, and when your body already tends toward internal Dampness and Heat from diet or constitution, a sticky, inflamed environment builds up. This Damp-Heat mixture clogs the hair follicles, weakens the roots, and leads to itching, flaking, and excessive shedding. Over time, the follicles become so congested that hair falls out and struggles to regrow.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow, greasy coating that is difficult to scrape off, often swollen with teeth marks. Pulse: slippery-rapid (滑数 huá shuò) or soggy-rapid (濡数 rú shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is like a steamy, sticky environment that clogs the hair follicles. Humid weather, heavy foods, and tight styles trap moisture and heat, making the scalp oily and inflamed. Cool, dry conditions, a clean scalp, and light meals help drain the Dampness and clear the Heat, allowing follicles to breathe and hair to regrow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sugary foods that generate Dampness and Heat. Eat more cooling, dampness-draining foods like barley, mung beans, cucumber, and bitter melon. Keep the scalp clean and dry, but avoid harsh shampoos. Loosen tight hairstyles to allow air circulation and reduce moisture buildup.

patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress and frustration cause Liver Qi to become stuck. Over time, this stagnant Qi congeals into Blood stasis, especially in the scalp where tight hairstyles already impair circulation. The trapped Blood fails to nourish hair follicles, leading to patchy hair loss that often comes with chest tightness and emotional tension.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots on the sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a knife scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work:
Emotional stress is the primary trigger because it directly causes Liver Qi to stagnate; over time, this stagnation congeals into Blood stasis that starves hair follicles. Relaxation, stress management, and gentle scalp massage help keep Qi and Blood moving, preventing stasis from taking hold.

Tight hairstyles add a mechanical layer of stagnation by physically compressing blood vessels in the scalp, making it harder for nutrient-rich Blood to reach the roots. Loosening these styles removes that barrier, while warmth on the scalp encourages vasodilation and better flow.

Foods that move Blood, like turmeric and hawthorn, work internally to break up stasis, while greasy and spicy foods can generate Dampness and Heat, which further obstruct circulation. The premenstrual phase is a time when Liver Qi and Blood are naturally more congested, so hair loss often flares then.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Loosen tight hairstyles to relieve traction on the scalp. Practice stress-reducing activities like gentle yoga or meditation to keep Liver Qi flowing smoothly. Include blood-moving foods in your diet such as turmeric, hawthorn berries, and dark leafy greens, and limit greasy or spicy foods that can generate heat and aggravate stagnation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Sparse, brittle hair with premature graying", "Lower back soreness and weak knees", "Dizziness and tinnitus", "Poor memory and difficulty concentrating", "Frequent urination at night"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and lack of sleep, Excessive sexual activity, Cold exposure, especially to the lower back, Tight hairstyles (braids, ponytails, weaves), Emotional stress or frustration
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and sleep, Nourishing foods (black sesame, walnuts, bone broth), Gentle movement (tai chi, walking), Keeping the lower back warm
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Essence is the deepest stored substance that fuels growth and nourishment, including the hair. Long-term or repeated traction slowly drains this reserve, like a well running dry. Without enough Essence to reach the scalp, hair roots become malnourished, leading to sparse, brittle strands and premature graying.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with little or no coating, possible fine cracks. Pulse: fine (thready) and deep, weak at both Chi (rear) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Essence is our deepest reserve; rest and nourishing foods replenish it, while overwork, excessive sexual activity, and cold drain it away. Tight hairstyles directly block Qi and blood flow to the scalp, compounding the deficiency. By removing the traction and supporting Essence, the hair roots can finally receive the nourishment they need to regrow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat foods that gently build Kidney Essence, such as black sesame seeds, walnuts, goji berries, and bone broths. Prioritize deep, restorative sleep and avoid overwork. Keep the lower back warm and consider gentle practices like tai chi or qi gong to preserve vitality. Most importantly, stop the tight hairstyles that triggered the problem.

patterns.why_this_happens: In traction alopecia, the external pulling already damages the hair. When the body lacks sufficient Qi and Blood, the scalp and hair follicles receive inadequate nourishment, making the hair weak, dry, and prone to falling out even with minimal tension. The Spleen, which produces Qi and Blood, is often weakened, so the body cannot generate enough Blood to anchor the hair roots, leading to excessive shedding with any traction.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, especially weak at the right Guan position (Spleen/Stomach).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are produced by the Spleen from food and rest. Raw, cold foods and overwork drain these resources, while warm, cooked meals and adequate sleep replenish them. Gentle scalp massage encourages local circulation without straining the body's energy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like bone broths, stews, cooked vegetables, and moderate amounts of red meat. Avoid raw, cold foods that tax the Spleen. Prioritize restful sleep and avoid overwork. Keep hairstyles loose to minimize mechanical stress on fragile hair.

faqs.question: How is TCM treatment for traction alopecia different from conventional approaches?
faqs.answer: Conventional treatment focuses on stopping the traction and sometimes using minoxidil to stimulate regrowth. TCM goes further by diagnosing the underlying pattern of imbalance that made your scalp vulnerable to the mechanical damage. For example, if your scalp is oily and itchy, we treat the Damp-Heat; if it's tender and the hair is brittle, we move Blood stasis. This internal approach, combined with acupuncture to directly improve local circulation, can accelerate healing and create a healthier environment for new hair to grow.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture alone stop my hair loss?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is a powerful tool for improving scalp circulation and reducing inflammation, but it works best as part of a comprehensive plan. Most traction alopecia patients benefit from a combination of acupuncture (1-2 times per week), daily herbal formulas, and lifestyle changes - especially loosening tight hairstyles. Acupuncture points on the scalp and body help unblock stagnation, while herbs address the deeper pattern. Some people do see reduced shedding with acupuncture alone, but for lasting regrowth, the internal imbalance must also be corrected.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Dietary adjustments support your treatment but don't have to be extreme. In general, avoid greasy, fried, and overly spicy foods that can generate Damp-Heat and worsen oily, itchy scalps. Focus on nourishing foods like black sesame seeds, walnuts, goji berries, dark leafy greens, and moderate amounts of high-quality protein. If your pattern involves Spleen weakness, you may also be advised to eat warm, cooked meals instead of cold, raw foods. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use herbal formulas while using minoxidil or other hair growth products?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM herbal formulas and acupuncture can generally be used alongside topical minoxidil or other conventional hair loss treatments. However, some Blood-moving herbs (such as Dang Gui and Chuan Xiong) may interact with anticoagulant medications, so it's crucial to inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about all treatments you're using. Always bring a full list of medications and supplements to your TCM consultation to ensure safety.

faqs.question: How long until I see new hair growth?
faqs.answer: Patience is essential. Hair grows slowly, and follicles that have been under chronic tension need time to recover. Most people notice reduced shedding and a healthier scalp within 4-8 weeks. The first fine, new hairs may appear around the 3-month mark, but significant visible regrowth often takes 6 months or longer. Consistency with herbs, acupuncture, and avoiding tight hairstyles is the key to success. If you've had traction alopecia for years, the timeline may be longer, but improvement is still possible.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if I've had traction alopecia for years and the hair follicles seem dead?
faqs.answer: Even long-standing traction alopecia can respond to TCM if there are still active follicles. Acupuncture and herbs work to revive dormant follicles by improving local blood flow and reducing inflammation. However, if scarring has occurred and follicles are permanently destroyed, regrowth may not be possible. A TCM practitioner can assess your scalp and give you a realistic prognosis. In many chronic cases, we see gradual improvement in hair density and quality, even if full regrowth isn't achieved.
